concepts.name: Token cost vs quality in multi-agent systems
When a multi-agent design is worth it
Delegating to subagents and scaling effort

questions.prompt: In Anthropic's multi-agent research system, what does the lead agent do?

choices.text: It routes each query to one specialist agent and returns that agent's answer unchanged
It hosts a shared chat where subagents negotiate with each other until they agree
It plans the research, spins up subagents in parallel on different parts, then combines their findings
It checks the subagents' spelling, while each subagent writes its own part of the final report

questions.explanation: The system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern: the lead agent (Claude Opus 4 in the post) decomposes the query, describes subtasks to subagents (Claude Sonnet 4) that search in parallel, and synthesises what they return. A separate CitationAgent then adds citations to the report. Subagents report to the lead; they don't coordinate with each other.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: A lead agent (Claude Opus 4) plans the research and delegates to Sonnet 4 subagents working in parallel, then compiles their results, with a CitationAgent adding citations afterwards.

sources.title: Building Effective AI Agents
sources.claim: In the orchestrator-workers pattern a central LLM breaks a task down, delegates to worker LLMs and synthesises their results.

questions.prompt: The post says the lead agent runs each set of subagents synchronously. What is the consequence?

choices.text: Coordination stays simple, but the lead waits for the slowest subagent and can't steer them mid-task
Subagents run one after another, so the system is never faster than a single agent
Subagents share one context window, so they can't run out of tokens
Results are deterministic, so the same query always gives the same report

questions.explanation: Synchronous here means the lead launches a set of subagents (in parallel with each other) and waits for all of them before continuing. Anthropic notes this simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks: the lead can't steer subagents, and the whole system waits on the slowest one. Parallel subagents and parallel tool calls still cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: Lead agents run subagents synchronously, waiting for each set to finish; this is simpler but means the lead can't steer subagents and the system can be blocked waiting on one subagent, while parallelism still cut research time by up to 90%.

questions.prompt: According to Anthropic's post, roughly how many tokens do agents and multi-agent systems use compared with a chat interaction?

choices.text: Agents about 1.5× and multi-agent systems about 3×
Agents about 4× and multi-agent systems about 15×
Agents about 10× and multi-agent systems about 100×
About the same, because subagents reuse the lead's cached context

questions.explanation: Anthropic reports that agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chats, and multi-agent systems about 15× more. That's why multi-agent designs only make economic sense for tasks valuable enough to pay for the extra tokens.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: Agents typically use about 4x more tokens than chat interactions and multi-agent systems about 15x more.

questions.prompt: In Anthropic's analysis of their BrowseComp results, which factor on its own explained about 80% of the variance in performance?

choices.text: Which model the lead agent used
How long the system prompt was
The number of subagents spawned
Token usage

questions.explanation: Three factors explained 95% of the variance, and token usage alone explained 80%; the number of tool calls and the model choice were the other two. The takeaway: multi-agent systems work largely because they spend more tokens in parallel, separate context windows, which is also why they cost more.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: On BrowseComp, three factors explained 95% of performance variance and token usage alone explained 80%, the others being number of tool calls and model choice.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: "When is a multi-agent design worth the extra tokens?" Answer using what Anthropic learned from its research system.

model_answer.summary: When the task is valuable enough to pay for many more tokens and splits into independent parts that can run in parallel, especially when the information won't fit in one context window; not when steps are tightly coupled.
key_points: Multi-agent systems use about 15× the tokens of a chat, so the task's value has to justify the cost
They excel at tasks with heavy parallelisation, such as breadth-first research across many sources
They help when the information exceeds a single context window, because each subagent has its own
They help when the task needs many complex tools
They fit poorly when agents need shared context or have many dependencies, such as most coding tasks

questions.explanation: Anthropic's own multi-agent system beat a single Opus 4 agent by 90.2% on their internal research eval, but they are explicit that this came from spending more tokens and that the approach suits parallel, high-value work. Naming both the benefit and the conditions is the answer interviewers want.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: Multi-agent systems use about 15x chat tokens and excel at valuable tasks with heavy parallelisation, information exceeding one context window, and many complex tools, but fit poorly where agents share context or have many dependencies, such as most coding tasks; the system beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2%.

sources.title: Building Effective AI Agents
sources.claim: Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, so developers should judge when that trade is worth it.

questions.prompt: Which task is the worst fit for a multi-agent design, according to Anthropic's post?

choices.text: Finding the board members of every company in a list of 50
Surveying recent papers on a topic from many independent sources
A refactor across tightly coupled modules where each change depends on the others
Comparing pricing and features of ten competing products

questions.explanation: The post says domains where agents need the same context or have many dependencies are a poor fit today, and that most coding tasks have fewer truly parallelisable parts than research. The other options split into independent searches, which is where parallel subagents shine.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: Domains requiring all agents to share the same context or involving many dependencies are a poor fit, and most coding tasks have fewer truly parallelisable parts than research.

questions.prompt: What should the lead agent include when it hands a subtask to a subagent?

choices.text: A short topic phrase only, so the subagent has the freedom to explore in its own direction
An objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries
The lead's entire conversation so far, so the subagent has every detail and nothing is lost
Just the output format, since the subagent can infer its objective and tools from that

questions.explanation: Anthropic found that short, vague instructions made subagents duplicate each other's work, leave gaps, or miss information. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear boundaries. Sending the whole transcript defeats the point of giving each subagent a clean context.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries; short vague instructions led to duplicated work, gaps, or missed information.

questions.prompt: Anthropic's prompts include rules for scaling effort to the query. How much effort do they give simple fact-finding?

choices.text: 3–5 subagents in parallel, as for every query
More than 10 subagents, to be safe
One agent with 3–10 tool calls
No tool calls: the lead answers from its own knowledge

questions.explanation: The rules: simple fact-finding needs 1 agent with 3–10 tool calls, direct comparisons 2–4 subagents with 10–15 calls each, and complex research possibly more than 10 subagents. Without such rules early agents spawned 50 subagents for simple queries. Effort scaling is how you keep the token bill in line with the task.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: Embedded scaling rules say simple fact-finding needs 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research possibly more than 10 subagents; early agents spawned 50 subagents for simple queries.

questions.prompt: This Lesson's exercise: design your own multi-agent research system. Describe its components and how a query flows through it.

model_answer.summary: A lead agent plans and delegates to parallel subagents with their own context windows, then synthesises their condensed findings; citations, memory and limits on effort complete the design.
key_points: The lead agent analyses the query, writes a plan, and saves it to memory so it survives if the context is truncated
It spawns subagents in parallel, each with an objective, output format, tool guidance and boundaries
Subagents search with their own tools and context windows and return condensed findings, not raw pages
The lead synthesises the findings, decides whether more research is needed, and a citation step attaches sources to claims
Effort rules cap subagents and tool calls by query complexity, and the system can resume after errors instead of starting over

questions.explanation: These are the parts Anthropic describes: planning with memory (context beyond 200,000 tokens gets truncated), parallel subagents, a CitationAgent, effort-scaling rules, and resuming from where errors occurred. A good design also says how it will be evaluated, which is the next concept.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: The lead agent saves its plan to Memory because context beyond 200,000 tokens is truncated, spawns parallel subagents that return filtered findings, decides whether more research is needed, hands off to a CitationAgent, follows effort-scaling rules, and the system resumes from where errors occurred.

questions.prompt: How did Anthropic find it most consistent to grade research reports with an LLM judge?

choices.text: A single LLM call with one rubric prompt, returning 0.0–1.0 scores and a pass-fail grade
A separate judge model for each rubric criterion, averaged at the end
Exact-match comparison against a reference report
Having the lead agent grade its own final report

questions.explanation: Anthropic tried multiple judges per component but found a single call with a single prompt, scoring 0.0–1.0 plus pass-fail, was the most consistent and best aligned with human judgement. The rubric covered factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality and tool efficiency. Exact match fails because many different reports can be correct.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: A single LLM call with a single prompt outputting 0.0-1.0 scores and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements; the rubric covered factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality and tool efficiency.

questions.prompt: Anthropic started evaluating its research agents with only about 20 real queries. Why was such a small set enough at first?

choices.text: LLM judges are accurate enough that the sample size barely affects what the evals show
Early changes have large effects (say 30% to 80% success from one prompt tweak), so few cases show them
Research queries are similar enough that 20 real ones cover nearly every kind of case that users will bring
Larger eval sets can't be run against multi-agent systems, because their runs are too costly

questions.explanation: In early development there's plenty of low-hanging fruit, so effects are big enough to see with a few test cases. Anthropic's advice is to start evaluating immediately with a small sample of real usage patterns rather than wait until you can build a large eval set. As effects get smaller, you need more cases.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: They began with about 20 queries representing real usage, because early on effect sizes are large (a prompt tweak might lift success from 30% to 80%), and advise starting evals immediately with small samples.

questions.prompt: How would you evaluate the outputs of your research system, given that there's no single correct report?

model_answer.summary: Judge the end result against a rubric with an LLM judge, starting with a small set of real queries, and keep humans testing to catch what automated evals miss.
key_points: Evaluate the final result (end state), not whether the agent followed a particular path, because valid runs take different routes
Use an LLM judge with a rubric such as factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality and tool efficiency
Start straight away with about 20 real queries, then grow the set as changes have smaller effects
Check the judge against human judgements before relying on it
Keep manual testing: Anthropic's testers found agents preferring SEO content farms over authoritative sources, which automated evals had missed

questions.explanation: Anthropic stresses that agents may search three sources or ten and still reach the same good answer, so grading the process is misleading. Human review found source-quality problems that the automated rubric didn't, which is why they kept both.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
sources.claim: Anthropic used end-state evaluation because agents take different valid paths (three sources vs ten), an LLM-judge rubric aligned with human judgement, started with ~20 real queries, and kept human testing, which caught agents preferring SEO content farms over authoritative sources.
